newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS-Budapest, Bucharest bourses hit records.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Budapest, Bucharest bourses hit records.

text.p: Budapest and Bucharest outperformed other central European markets this week as they hit record highs on the back of fresh capital.
Prague also firmed although political uncertainties remained, while Warsaw reversed from falls to end the week with meagre gains. Ljubljana and Bratislava eased while Zageb was mixed.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which measures price movements in 72 Czech, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak and Slovenian shares, edged up.
BUDAPEST
A five-day string of record closes on the Budapest Stock Exchange continued on Friday as demand absorbed shares unloaded by arbitrageurs between the cash and the futures markets.

The market ended the week in a positive tone and analysts said the Hungarian government's decision on Thursday to reduce its stakes to "golden shares" in key firms will have a beneficial impact on longer term.

"The government's decision to bring down state shareholdings to the lowest level possible in what were previously considered strategic companies will be an important step," said Spencer Jakab, analyst at CS First Boston in Budapest.
BUCHAREST

Most Bucharest stocks rose over the week due to fresh foreign interest in Romanian equities after the government aproved for the first time rules on portfolio investments. On Friday, all first-tier listings closed firmer under buying pressure.

The unofficial VAB index, computed by market capitalisation and average prices, rose by 3.8 percent, while another independent index, the BIG, gained 9.02 percent from Thursday to reach a new year-high.
PRAGUE

A return of foreign investors pushed Czech share prices higher for most of the week before renewed political uncertainty forced most on to the sidelines. The Prague bourse's PX50 index ended on Friday at 497.6, up 9.0 on the week.
Dealers said interest in several blue chips had given rise to a wave of optimism that prices had fallen to levels that made them too attractive to pass up.
But a confidence vote called for next Tuesday coupled with infighting among the governing coalition squelched what little momentum the market had gained.

"It looks like many investors are going to wait to see the result of the confidence vote and then, based on that, they will either take or not take positions," said Lubos Vystavel, a trader at ING Barings in Prague.
WARSAW
Polish shares recovered on Friday, after falls earlier in the week on large sales on the primary market and analysts expected growth at least in the beginning of next week in reaction to the falls.

But they said the upside was limited as the primary market was drawing investor capital and attention to offers such as those of Bank Handlowy, in which one billion zlotys worth of shares are on sale, and copper giant KGHM expected later in June.
"The market might rise at the beginning of the week but later there might be falls in profit-taking," said Grzegorz Cimochowski, an analyst at ING Barings.
Analysts said that in the longer-term the market might keep its sideways drift until elections, expected in September.
BRATISLAVA
Trading on the Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) was quiet throughout the week with dealers anticipating little change until the liquidity squeeze on the interbank market eases off.
"I don't expect this situation to improve unless some liquidity appears in the system," Peter Krutil of Creditanstalt Securities said.

The Slovak central bank has been keeping the interbank market short of liquidity as a means of protecting the crown. However, equities dealers say this has had the knock-on effect of choking off funds for dealing in shares.
LJUBLJANA

Slovenian shares eased 1.07 percent this week to 1,309.19 points on Friday and traders said a falling trend was likely to continue over the summer as no fresh foreign money or information that could boost prices was expected.

Market participants said future movements on the market would largely depend on ratification of the EU association accord signed June 1996 as it would attract international investors to resume their activity.

"I am afraid foreign players are already losing their patience and according to my information some of them are already switching to neighbouring markets that are apparently more attractive," said Jasna Zontar, trader at brokerage Modra.

On Thursday the Constitutional Court said parliament could not ratify the EU accord because it contravened the constitutional article that prohibits foreigners owning land in Slovenia, thus delaying the ratification.
ZAGREB

Food concern Podravka led Croatian stocks on Friday and traders predicted the situation would remain quiet in the coming days. "Podravka will continue trading well next week, the rest will be boring," one trader said.
